column2: But they had landed on the wrong side of the island. The whaling station at Stromness was on the other side, across the mountains.
The boat was too damaged to sail around. Nobody had ever crossed the island's mountains on foot.
They rested and ate for nine days. Then, on the nineteenth of May, Shackleton, Worsley and Crean set off. Three men stayed with the boat.
McNish had pulled screws from the boat and fixed them into their boots for grip. They carried no tents and no sleeping bags.
Again and again they climbed a ridge, found a sheer drop on the other side, and had to turn back.
Night was falling on a high ridge. If they stayed, they would freeze. So they coiled the rope into sledges, sat down, and slid down the mountain in the dark.
At seven in the morning, they heard a steam whistle. The whalers at Stromness were being called to work.
On the twentieth of May 1916, after thirty-six hours of walking, three men with black faces and long beards walked into the whaling station.
The station manager knew Shackleton well. He did not recognise him. Then Shackleton said his name.
Nobody crossed South Georgia on foot again until 1955, and those were trained mountaineers with full equipment.
That night, a whaling boat went round to King Haakon Bay and picked up the other three men.
